title: Time every shot by its reads: what the viewer must understand, one at a time
when: Planning the length and order of what happens inside each shot.
summary: The viewer sees each moment once, at full speed, for the first time. List in order what they must understand (each is a 'read'), give each read time to be found, understood and registered, and never start the next read while the last is still landing. The reads set the shot's length.
steps: For each shot, write its reads in order in the shot's notes.
Give small, far or subtle reads more time than big central ones.
Put a cause and its reaction one after the other, not on top of each other.
Lengthen the shot or cut a read when they do not fit; never squeeze them.
avoid: Two important things happening at once.
Padding a shot whose reads have all landed.
checks: No two important reads overlap in time.
The last read of the video has time to land before the end.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (JohnHeibel, MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: ANIMATION_GUIDE rule 4 and the storyboard format; restated.

title: Something happens in every shot
when: Drawing story shots with characters or objects.
summary: A shot is not a picture; something changes between its first and last frame. A character wants, finds, tries, fails, reacts or gets. 'A figure stands in a field' is not a shot.
do: Name the event of each story shot in its notes.
Stage one focal action at a time with a clear silhouette.
Show cause, then reaction, and give the reaction time: it is often the best part.
Pay off what a shot sets up, in that shot or a later one.
checks: Each story shot has a named event.

title: Act it, do not label it
when: Deciding whether a moment needs words on screen.
summary: A sign or label that repeats the story is a classic failure: a figure holding a sign that says 'lost' instead of looking left, then right, the map upside down, a bead of sweat. Words on screen are for key words, names and numbers the narration stresses, never for what acting can show.
do: Show an emotion through pose, face and a small action.
Keep on-screen words for the key word, a name or a figure.
avoid: A label that names what the picture already shows.
Speech bubbles that repeat the narration.
checks: No label repeats what the drawing already makes obvious.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: rule 2, adapted to this program's key-words-on-screen standard.

title: Nothing is ever still: idle motion, drifting camera, breathing world
when: Any held shot or pause in the action.
summary: A frozen frame reads as a bug. Every emotion has its own idle motion, cameras drift or push a little, the world breathes: grass sways, smoke rises, a light flickers.
do: Give every held character an idle that matches its emotion.
Let the camera drift or push slightly on held shots.
Add one small living detail to every place.
avoid: A motionless frame longer than about half a second outside the final card.
checks: No held stretch longer than about 0.6 s without motion.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: rule 5; motion-video-kit (MIT) pacing numbers; restated.

title: Faces act through a change, they never snap
when: A character's emotion changes inside a shot.
summary: An emotion change is a small performance: a beat of anticipation, a squint or blink, the take, a small overshoot, then the settle. Swapping the face in one frame reads as a glitch.
steps: Anticipate with a small opposite move or a blink.
Make the take larger than the final expression.
avoid: Changing eyes and mouth between two frames with nothing in between.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: rule 5 and emotions; restated.

title: Anticipation, weight and arcs
when: Planning any character move, prop throw, jump, turn or entrance.
summary: Before a big move, a small move the other way tells the viewer where to look. How a thing starts and stops says what it weighs: heavy things are slow to start and stop and barely bounce, light things snap and flutter. Living things move on arcs, not straight lines.
do: Add a wind-up before a throw, a crouch before a jump.
Ease into and out of poses; linear motion only for machines.
Move hands, heads and thrown things on arcs.
Match start, stop and bounce to the object's weight.
avoid: Everything moving at one brisk, constant speed.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: animation principles; synfig and OpenToonz waypoint easing (ideas only); restated.

title: Overlap the parts and avoid twinning
when: Animating bodies, crowds or groups of objects.
summary: Code moves every part at once on the same curve, so motion looks mechanical. Eyes lead, the body follows, and hats, tails and props drag and settle last. Both arms at the same angle, a crowd bouncing in unison or both eyes blinking together all read as machine-made.
do: Offset the timing of parts from the part they hang off.
Give one arm the action and the other a smaller move.
Offset phases and timings between characters in a group.
checks: No two characters in a shot move in perfect unison.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: overlapping action and twinning; restated.

title: Strong key poses that read as stills, then motion between them
when: Choosing the poses of characters in a shot.
summary: If the key poses do not read as stills, no motion will fix them. Each storytelling pose has a clear silhouette and leans into what the character is doing; push it further than feels natural, because subtle reads as nothing.
steps: Pick the 1-3 storytelling poses of the shot.
Check each reads as a silhouette.
Exaggerate the pose, then pull back only if it looks wrong.
Show the thought: the character notices, thinks, then acts, eyes first.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: strong key poses, exaggeration, show the thought; restated.

title: Every seam gets a transition that belongs to the story
when: Choosing how one shot or scene becomes the next.
summary: Pick transitions from what is happening: a match cut on a shape or motion, a cut on action that finishes the move in the next shot, a camera move that carries into the next shot, an iris on what matters. Do not default to the same transition every time.
do: Prefer a match cut or a cut on action between related shots.
Use a shaped or carried transition at scene changes.
Keep a plain cut for action or deliberate smash cuts.

title: One film: one world, a colour arc, an ending that rhymes
when: Planning the whole video's look and emotional line.
summary: A video is one short film, not a pile of clips. Keep one world and palette, move the colour along the emotion (cold to warm as things improve), carry screen direction and props across cuts, and rhyme the ending with the opening: the same place, pose or motif, changed.
do: Plan the emotional keys across the whole video, not per shot.
Let the palette shift with the story's arc.
Return to the opening image, changed, at the end.
checks: The last scene echoes the first.

title: Depth from overlap, scale and layers, never fake 3D
summary: Flat drawn worlds get depth from overlap (near things cover far ones), scale (far things smaller), value (far things lighter and softer) and layers moving at different speeds with the camera. Projecting 3D on flat drawings looks wrong.
do: Put something behind, the action in the middle, and one thing near the camera.
Make far layers lighter, softer and slower with the camera.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT) rule 1; PixiJS (MIT) scene graph and containers, ideas only; restated.

title: Light adds, paint mixes: glows go on top
when: Drawing fire, sparks, lamps, magic, screens or any glowing thing.
summary: Paint mixes like pigment, so a yellow glow painted over blue turns green. Light adds: glows and highlights are drawn in an additive or screen blend on top of the picture.
do: Draw glows with a screen or additive blend.
Keep glows soft and centred on their source.
avoid: Painting light as an opaque yellow shape over a dark scene.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT) light exception; PixiJS (MIT) blend modes, ideas only; restated.

title: Hold drawings on twos for a hand-made feel; ones for fast action
when: Choosing the frame cadence of hand-made looks.
summary: Traditional animation exposes each drawing for two frames (twos) in normal action and one frame (ones) for fast or smooth moves. A hand-made look on twos feels drawn; everything on ones feels digital. Camera moves stay smooth on ones even when the drawing is on twos.
do: Use twos for character acting in hand-made looks.
Switch to ones for fast action and smooth camera moves.
avoid: Twos on a camera pan, which judders.
source: OpenToonz (BSD-3) exposure sheet and synfig (GPL-3.0) timing, ideas only; restated.

title: Move limbs by rotating at the joints
when: Posing or animating figures and articulated objects.
summary: Arms, legs, heads and hinged objects move by rotating around their joints, the way a skeleton drives a cut-out character. Sliding a limb in a straight line breaks the body.
do: Rotate limbs around shoulder, elbow, hip and knee.
Move the parent joint first and let children follow.
avoid: Translating a hand straight across the frame without the arm following.
source: synfig (GPL-3.0) skeleton layers, ideas only; restated.

title: Particles in small, varied, purposeful bursts
when: Drawing sparks, dust, snow, leaves, confetti or rain.
summary: Many small sprites read as a living effect when each has its own size, speed, spin and lifetime, and when the effect starts and ends with the action that causes it.
do: Vary size, speed, spin and lifetime per particle from a seed.
Tie the burst to its cause and let it fade naturally.
avoid: Endless loops of identical particles behind everything.
source: PixiJS (MIT) particle containers, ideas only; restated.

title: Review by contact sheets and strips, not by intention
when: Checking drawn shots, designed shots or a rendered video.
summary: Look at the work itself: the first, middle and last frame of every shot to see the whole shape, every frame of a key moment (turns, takes, throws, transitions) to catch pops, and full-size crops of faces and hands.
steps: Sheet: first, middle and last frame of each shot.
Strip: every frame across each transition and big action.
Crops: faces, hands and contacts at full size.
avoid: Approving from the plan instead of the frames.
source: ClaudeAnimationBase (MIT), pinned 0ac8bf2: the review loop; restated.
